# Produce submission

def create_submission(confidence_scores, save_path):
    '''Creates an output file of submissions for Kaggle

    Parameters
    ----------
    confidence_scores : list or numpy array
        Confidence scores (from predict_proba methods from classifiers) or
        binary predictions (only recommended in cases when predict_proba is
        not available)
    save_path : string
        File path for where to save the submission file.

    Example:
    create_submission(my_confidence_scores, './data/submission.csv')

    '''
    submission = pd.DataFrame({"score":confidence_scores})
    submission.to_csv(save_path, index_label="id")

# feature engineering - add total guests, total nights, total costs, booking changes, is family?
def add_features(df):
    df = df.copy()

    df["total_guests"] = (
        df["adults"] +
        df["children"].fillna(0) +
        df["babies"]
    )

    df["total_nights"] = (
        df["stays_in_weekend_nights"] +
        df["stays_in_week_nights"]
    )

    df["total_cost"] = df["adr"] * df["total_nights"]

    df["booking_changes_ratio"] = (
        df["booking_changes"] / (df["lead_time"] + 1)
    )

    df["is_family"] = (
        (df["children"].fillna(0) + df["babies"]) > 0
    ).astype(int)

    df = df.drop(columns=["agent", "company"], errors="ignore")
    return df

In preprocessing, I first did feature engineering to add more informative variables: total guests, total nights, total cost to capture more information about booking. I added booking changes ratio to normalize the changes by lead time, and an indicator for whether it is a family/household. These features could help the model learn more patterns. I dropped the features agent and company because those seem like they could be adding more noise than useful.

The data was already provided as one hot encoded which was important for transforming categorical data into features we can use for models. The data is split into training and validation sets with stratification so that the class distirbution is preserved. I handle missing values using median imputation since that is robust to outliers and can prevent data leakage by fitting only on trainng data and applying that to validation/test sets. I use standardization to make sure the features are on the same scale, which is important for models sensitive to feature magnitude (such as logistic regression,SVMs, KNN).

1.3: Train and Compare Models¶

In [ ]:
# store model results
results = []

def evaluate_model(name, model, X_tr, y_tr, X_v, y_v):
    # training time
    train_start = time.perf_counter()
    model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    train_end = time.perf_counter()
    train_time = train_end - train_start

    # inference time
    pred_start = time.perf_counter()
    y_val_pred = model.predict(X_v)

    if hasattr(model, "predict_proba"):
        y_val_score = model.predict_proba(X_v)[:, 1]
    elif hasattr(model, "decision_function"):
        y_val_score = model.decision_function(X_v)
    else:
        y_val_score = y_val_pred

    pred_end = time.perf_counter()
    pred_time = pred_end - pred_start

    # evaluation metrics
    acc = accuracy_score(y_v, y_val_pred)
    auc = roc_auc_score(y_v, y_val_score)
    ap = average_precision_score(y_v, y_val_score)

    # roc curve points
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_v, y_val_score)

    # precision recall curve points
    precision, recall, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_v, y_val_score)

    # save results
    results.append({
        "Model": name,
        "Validation Accuracy": acc,
        "Validation AUC": auc,
        "Validation AP": ap,
        "Training Time (s)": train_time,
        "Prediction Time (s)": pred_time,
        "fpr": fpr,
        "tpr": tpr,
        "precision": precision,
        "recall": recall
    })

    # print summary
    print(f"{name}")
    print(f"  Accuracy:        {acc:.4f}")
    print(f"  ROC AUC:         {auc:.4f}")
    print(f"  Average Precision: {ap:.4f}")
    print(f"  Training Time:   {train_time:.4f} s")
    print(f"  Prediction Time: {pred_time:.4f} s\n")

    return model


def plot_roc_curves(results):
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))

    for res in results:
        plt.plot(
            res["fpr"],
            res["tpr"],
            label=f'{res["Model"]} (AUC = {res["Validation AUC"]:.3f})'
        )

    # line to show guessing at random
    plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", label="Random Guessing")

    plt.xlabel("False Positive Rate")
    plt.ylabel("True Positive Rate")
    plt.title("ROC Curves on Validation Data")
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.show()


def plot_pr_curves(results, y_v):
    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))

    for res in results:
        plt.plot(
            res["recall"],
            res["precision"],
            label=f'{res["Model"]} (AP = {res["Validation AP"]:.3f})'
        )

    # line to show guessing at random
    baseline = np.mean(y_v)
    plt.axhline(y=baseline, linestyle="--", label=f"Random Guessing ({baseline:.3f})")

    plt.xlabel("Recall")
    plt.ylabel("Precision")
    plt.title("Precision-Recall Curves on Validation Data")
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True)
    plt.show()



def plot_model_times(results):
    results_df = pd.DataFrame(results)

    plot_df = results_df[["Model", "Training Time (s)", "Prediction Time (s)"]].copy()
    plot_df = plot_df.sort_values("Training Time (s)", ascending=False)

    x = np.arange(len(plot_df))
    width = 0.35

    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    plt.bar(x - width/2, plot_df["Training Time (s)"], width, label="Training Time")
    plt.bar(x + width/2, plot_df["Prediction Time (s)"], width, label="Prediction Time")

    plt.xticks(x, plot_df["Model"], rotation=45, ha="right")
    plt.ylabel("Time (seconds)")
    plt.title("Training and Prediction Time by Model")
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(axis="y")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


def results_table(results):
    df = pd.DataFrame(results)[[
        "Model",
        "Validation Accuracy",
        "Validation AUC",
        "Validation AP",
        "Training Time (s)",
        "Prediction Time (s)"
    ]].copy()

    return df.sort_values("Validation AUC", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

# lightGBM with Optuna

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)

def lgbm_objective(trial):
    params = {
        "n_estimators":    trial.suggest_int("n_estimators", 300, 1200),
        "learning_rate":   trial.suggest_float("learning_rate", 0.01, 0.15, log=True),
        "num_leaves":      trial.suggest_int("num_leaves", 31, 255),
        "max_depth":       trial.suggest_int("max_depth", 4, 10),
        "min_child_samples": trial.suggest_int("min_child_samples", 10, 100),
        "subsample":       trial.suggest_float("subsample", 0.6, 1.0),
        "colsample_bytree": trial.suggest_float("colsample_bytree", 0.6, 1.0),
        "reg_alpha":       trial.suggest_float("reg_alpha", 1e-4, 10.0, log=True),
        "reg_lambda":      trial.suggest_float("reg_lambda", 1e-4, 10.0, log=True),
        "random_state": 42,
        "n_jobs": -1,
        "verbosity": -1,
    }
    clf = lgb.LGBMClassifier(**params)
    clf.fit(
        X_train_imputed, y_train_split,
        eval_set=[(X_val_imputed, y_val)],
    )
    val_probs = clf.predict_proba(X_val_imputed)[:, 1]
    return roc_auc_score(y_val, val_probs)

study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize")
study.optimize(lgbm_objective, n_trials=40, show_progress_bar=True)

print("Best LightGBM CV AUC:", study.best_value)
print("Best params:", study.best_params)

best_lgbm = lgb.LGBMClassifier(
    **study.best_params,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbosity=-1,
)

best_lgbm = evaluate_model(
    "LightGBM (Optuna)",
    best_lgbm,
    X_train_imputed, y_train_split,
    X_val_imputed, y_val,
)

estimators = [
    ("xgb", XGBClassifier(
        n_estimators=800, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=6,
        subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8, min_child_weight=3,

    )),
]

stack_clf = StackingClassifier(
    estimators=estimators,
    final_estimator=LR(C=1.0, max_iter=1000),
    cv=5,
    stack_method="predict_proba",
    n_jobs=-1,
    passthrough=False,
)

stack_clf = evaluate_model(
    "Stacking (XGB+LGBM+RF)",
    stack_clf,
    X_train_imputed, y_train_split,
    X_val_imputed, y_val,
)

Model selection & tuning: I started with baseline models (logistic regression (plus adding regularization), KNN) and then moved to more complex tree-based models (Random Forests, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM). I used a validation split with ROC-AUC as the main metric and compared PR/ROC curves. For tuning, I applied manual tuning (e.g., depth, estimators), early stopping for XGBoost to find optimal trees, and Optuna for LightGBM to systematically search hyperparameters. I also tried a stacking ensemble combining top models. I had tried a grid search at first for Random Forest but due to computational limits, was unable to complete it, which is why I pivoted to trying gradient boosting models instead.

Best model & selection: LightGBM (Optuna) performed best (highest AUC ≈ 0.958 and strongest PR curve), closely followed by stacking and XGBoost. I selected it based on consistently highest validation AUC and better precision-recall tradeoff across thresholds, indicating stronger performance on imbalanced data.

1.3 Applying Model¶

Exercise 2: Clustering¶

2.1: K Means¶

In [7]:
################################
# Load the data
################################
import os
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs, make_moons

# Create / load the datasets:
n_samples = 1500
X0, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=n_samples, centers=2, n_features=2, random_state=0)
X1, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=n_samples, centers=5, n_features=2, random_state=0)

random_state = 170
X, y = make_blobs(n_samples=n_samples, random_state=random_state, cluster_std=1.3)
transformation = [[0.6, -0.6], [-0.2, 0.8]]
X2 = np.dot(X, transformation)
X3, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=n_samples, cluster_std=[1.0, 2.5, 0.5], random_state=random_state)
X4, _ = make_moons(n_samples=n_samples, noise=.12)

X = [X0, X1, X2, X3, X4]
# The datasets are X[i], where i ranges from 0 to 4


################################
# Code to plot clusters
################################
def plot_cluster(ax, data, cluster_assignments):
    '''Plot two-dimensional data clusters

    Parameters
    ----------
    ax : matplotlib axis
        Axis to plot on
    data : list or numpy array of size [N x 2]
        Clustered data
    cluster_assignments : list or numpy array [N]
        Cluster assignments for each point in data

    '''
    clusters = np.unique(cluster_assignments)
    n_clusters = len(clusters)
    for ca in clusters:
        kwargs = {}
        if ca == -1:
            # if samples are not assigned to a cluster (have a cluster assignment of -1, color them gray)
            kwargs = {'color':'gray'}
            n_clusters = n_clusters - 1
        ax.scatter(data[cluster_assignments==ca, 0], data[cluster_assignments==ca, 1],s=5,alpha=0.5, **kwargs)
        ax.set_xlabel('feature 1')
        ax.set_ylabel('feature 2')
        ax.set_title(f'No. Clusters = {n_clusters}')
        ax.axis('equal')

# scatter plot each dataset
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(22, 4))
for i, data in enumerate(X):
    axes[i].scatter(data[:, 0], data[:, 1], s=5, alpha=0.5)
    axes[i].set_title(f"Dataset {i}")
    axes[i].set_xlabel("feature 1")
    axes[i].set_ylabel("feature 2")
    axes[i].axis("equal")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans, DBSCAN, SpectralClustering
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

k_values = range(1, 11)
inertias = {}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(22, 4))
for i, data in enumerate(X):
    dataset_inertias = []
    for k in k_values:
        km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=0, n_init=10)
        km.fit(data)
        dataset_inertias.append(km.inertia_)
    inertias[i] = dataset_inertias

    axes[i].plot(list(k_values), dataset_inertias, marker='o')
    axes[i].set_title(f"Dataset {i} Elbow Curve")
    axes[i].set_xlabel("k")
    axes[i].set_ylabel("inertia")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

k_values = range(2, 11)  # silhouette not defined for k=1
silhouette_scores = {}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(22, 4))

for i, data in enumerate(X):
    scores = []

    for k in k_values:
        km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=0, n_init=10)
        labels = km.fit_predict(data)
        score = silhouette_score(data, labels)
        scores.append(score)

    silhouette_scores[i] = scores

    axes[i].plot(list(k_values), scores, marker='o')
    axes[i].set_title(f"Dataset {i} Silhouette")
    axes[i].set_xlabel("k")
    axes[i].set_ylabel("score")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

best_k_silhouette = {}

for i in range(len(X)):
    scores = silhouette_scores[i]
    best_k = list(k_values)[np.argmax(scores)]
    best_k_silhouette[i] = best_k

print(best_k_silhouette)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(22, 4))

for i, data in enumerate(X):
    k = best_k_silhouette[i]
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=0, n_init=10)
    labels = km.fit_predict(data)

    plot_cluster(axes[i], data, labels)
    axes[i].set_title(f"Dataset {i}, k = {k}")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

{0: 2, 1: 2, 2: 2, 3: 3, 4: 2}

Interpretation:

From the elbow curves for each dataset (dataset 0, 1, 2, 4), the elbow appears at k=2 (except for dataset 3 which performed better with k=3 clusters), which indicates this is where the inertia begins to have diminishing returns as we increase number of clusters, and this value of k could be a good balance.

2.2: DBSCAN¶

In [8]:
# change  eps and min_samples parameters to get as close as you can to having the same number of clusters as your choices with K-means
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN

eps_values = np.linspace(0.1, 1.5, 15)
min_samples_values = [3, 5, 10, 15]

best_dbscan_params = {}
best_dbscan_labels = {}

# search for the best dbscan params to get as close to number of clusters as above
for i, data in enumerate(X):

    # number of cluster choices for each dataset from kmeans
    target_k = best_k_silhouette[i]
    best_diff = float("inf")
    best_params = None
    best_labels = None

    for eps in eps_values:
        for min_samples in min_samples_values:
            db = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=min_samples)
            labels = db.fit_predict(data)

            n_clusters = len(set(labels)) - (1 if -1 in labels else 0)
            diff = abs(n_clusters - target_k)

            if diff < best_diff:
                best_diff = diff
                best_params = (eps, min_samples, n_clusters)
                best_labels = labels

    best_dbscan_params[i] = best_params
    best_dbscan_labels[i] = best_labels

for i in range(len(X)):
    eps, min_samples, n_clusters = best_dbscan_params[i]
    print(f"Dataset {i}: target k = {best_k_silhouette[i]}, eps = {eps:.2f}, min_samples = {min_samples}, DBSCAN clusters = {n_clusters}")

Dataset 0: target k = 2, eps = 0.30, min_samples = 10, DBSCAN clusters = 2
Dataset 1: target k = 2, eps = 0.50, min_samples = 5, DBSCAN clusters = 2
Dataset 2: target k = 2, eps = 0.10, min_samples = 10, DBSCAN clusters = 2
Dataset 3: target k = 3, eps = 0.30, min_samples = 10, DBSCAN clusters = 3
Dataset 4: target k = 2, eps = 0.10, min_samples = 3, DBSCAN clusters = 2
In [9]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(22, 4))
fig.suptitle("DBSCAN")

for i, data in enumerate(X):
    plot_cluster(axes[i], data, best_dbscan_labels[i])
    eps, min_samples, n_clusters = best_dbscan_params[i]
    axes[i].set_title(f"Dataset {i}\neps={eps:.2f}, min_samples={min_samples}")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

2.3: Spectral Clustering¶

In [10]:
#Apply Spectral Clustering. Select the same number of clusters as selected by k-means.
from sklearn.cluster import SpectralClustering

sc_labels = {}


for i, data in enumerate(X):

    # number of cluster choices for each dataset from kmeans
    target_k = best_k_silhouette[i]

    sc = SpectralClustering(
    n_clusters=target_k,
    affinity='nearest_neighbors',
    n_neighbors=10,
    random_state=42
)
    labels = sc.fit_predict(data)
    sc_labels[i] = labels


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(22, 4))
fig.suptitle("Spectral Clustering")

for i, data in enumerate(X):
    plot_cluster(axes[i], data, sc_labels[i])
    axes[i].set_title(f"Dataset {i}\n")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Interpretation:

On the more simple structured blob datasets (0, 1, and 3), KMeans worked well without much tuning needed beyond choosing k. However, on dataset 2, KMeans did not perform as well with the elongated clusters in dataset 2 and on the moons dataset 4. DBSCAN worked very well on dataset 4 as it could capture those non-linear shapes, but it was inconsident on the other datasets, especially dataset2 and 3. And DBSCAN required the most tuning for eps and min_samples, which are sensitive. Spectral Clustering seemed to be consistent across all datasets, as it performed similar to Kmeans on the simple data while also doing well on the non-linear data structures as well. KMeans is the easiest but least flexible, while DBSCAN is the hardest to tune and good for complex shapes, but overall, Spectral Clustering has the best balance.

In [10]:

Exercise 3 - Dimensionality Reduction¶

In [11]:
################################
# Load the data
################################
from sklearn import datasets
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE

# load dataset
digits = datasets.load_digits()
n_sample = digits.target.shape[0]
n_feature = digits.images.shape[1] * digits.images.shape[2]
X_digits = np.zeros((n_sample, n_feature))
for i in range(n_sample):
    X_digits[i, :] = digits.images[i, :, :].flatten()
y_digits = digits.target

3.1: PCA¶

In [12]:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
# standardize before PCA / t-SNE
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_digits)

# pca to 2d
pca_2d = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=42)
X_pca_2d = pca_2d.fit_transform(X_scaled)

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 7))
scatter = plt.scatter(X_pca_2d[:, 0], X_pca_2d[:, 1], c=y_digits, cmap="tab10", s=18, alpha=0.8)
plt.xlabel("PC1")
plt.ylabel("PC2")
plt.title("Digits dataset projected to 2D with PCA")
plt.legend(*scatter.legend_elements(), title="Digit")
plt.show()

I standardized the digits data before PCA because PCA is variance-based, so features on larger scales can dominate the principal components. After reducing the data to 2 dimensions, the PCA plot shows some visible grouping by digit, but several classes still overlap because projecting to only two linear components loses a large amount of information.

3.2: Plot Variance Explained¶

In [13]:
# cumulative explained variance
pca_full = PCA().fit(X_scaled)
cum_var = np.cumsum(pca_full.explained_variance_ratio_)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(range(1, len(cum_var) + 1), cum_var, marker="o")
plt.xlabel("Number of principal components")
plt.ylabel("Cumulative explained variance ratio")
plt.title("PCA cumulative explained variance")
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

unexplained_2pc = 1 - cum_var[1]
print("Fraction unexplained by first 2 PCs:", unexplained_2pc)

Fraction unexplained by first 2 PCs: 0.7840502949916721

The cumulative explained variance plot shows how much total variance is captured as more principal components are added. The fraction of variance unexplained by the first two principal components is 1 - cumulative variance at 2 PCs, which here is the printed value above (0.784). Since a large fraction of the variance is unexplained, the 2D PCA visualization cannot perfectly separate the digits, so overlap between classes is expected.

3.3: t-SNE¶

In [14]:
# t-SNE to 2D
tsne = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, random_state=42, init="pca", learning_rate="auto")
X_tsne_2d = tsne.fit_transform(X_scaled)

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 7))
scatter = plt.scatter(X_tsne_2d[:, 0], X_tsne_2d[:, 1], c=y_digits, cmap="tab10", s=18, alpha=0.8)
plt.xlabel("t-SNE 1")
plt.ylabel("t-SNE 2")
plt.title("Digits dataset projected to 2D with t-SNE")
plt.legend(*scatter.legend_elements(), title="Digit")
plt.show()

t-SNE gives a 2D embedding that is usually much better at separating the digit classes visually because it is able to preserve local neighborhood structure instead of maximizing global variance. In the t-SNE plot, the classes tend to form tighter and more distinct groups than in PCA.

3.4: Conclusion¶

TSNE clusters the data better than PCA because the dataset has non linear structure so PCA can't fully capture this wth only 2 linear components. PCA is faster and simpler however, with more interpretable explained variance whle TSNE is good for visualization but requires more computation. That is why in scikit learn, TSNE usualy has fit_transform and not a separate transform, as it does not provide a true transform for new points. The embedding comes from the full dataset so adding new points isn't added in the same way that PCA does.

    Name of the template to use
    Default: ''
    Equivalent to: [--TemplateExporter.template_name]
--template-file=<Unicode>
    Name of the template file to use
    Default: None
    Equivalent to: [--TemplateExporter.template_file]
--theme=<Unicode>
    Template specific theme(e.g. the name of a JupyterLab CSS theme distributed
    as prebuilt extension for the lab template)
    Default: 'light'
    Equivalent to: [--HTMLExporter.theme]
--sanitize_html=<Bool>
    Whether the HTML in Markdown cells and cell outputs should be sanitized.This
    should be set to True by nbviewer or similar tools.
    Default: False
    Equivalent to: [--HTMLExporter.sanitize_html]
--writer=<DottedObjectName>
    Writer class used to write the
                                        results of the conversion
    Default: 'FilesWriter'
    Equivalent to: [--NbConvertApp.writer_class]
--post=<DottedOrNone>
    PostProcessor class used to write the
                                        results of the conversion
    Default: ''
    Equivalent to: [--NbConvertApp.postprocessor_class]
--output=<Unicode>
    Overwrite base name use for output files.
                Supports pattern replacements '{notebook_name}'.
    Default: '{notebook_name}'
    Equivalent to: [--NbConvertApp.output_base]
--output-dir=<Unicode>
    Directory to write output(s) to. Defaults
                                  to output to the directory of each notebook. To recover
                                  previous default behaviour (outputting to the current
                                  working directory) use . as the flag value.
    Default: ''
    Equivalent to: [--FilesWriter.build_directory]
--reveal-prefix=<Unicode>
    The URL prefix for reveal.js (version 3.x).
            This defaults to the reveal CDN, but can be any url pointing to a copy
            of reveal.js.
            For speaker notes to work, this must be a relative path to a local
            copy of reveal.js: e.g., "reveal.js".
            If a relative path is given, it must be a subdirectory of the
            current directory (from which the server is run).
            See the usage documentation
            (https://nbconvert.readthedocs.io/en/latest/usage.html#reveal-js-html-slideshow)
            for more details.
    Default: ''
    Equivalent to: [--SlidesExporter.reveal_url_prefix]
--nbformat=<Enum>
    The nbformat version to write.
            Use this to downgrade notebooks.
    Choices: any of [1, 2, 3, 4]
    Default: 4
    Equivalent to: [--NotebookExporter.nbformat_version]

Examples
--------

    The simplest way to use nbconvert is

            > jupyter nbconvert mynotebook.ipynb --to html

            Options include ['asciidoc', 'custom', 'html', 'latex', 'markdown', 'notebook', 'pdf', 'python', 'qtpdf', 'qtpng', 'rst', 'script', 'slides', 'webpdf'].

            > jupyter nbconvert --to latex mynotebook.ipynb

            Both HTML and LaTeX support multiple output templates. LaTeX includes
            'base', 'article' and 'report'.  HTML includes 'basic', 'lab' and
            'classic'. You can specify the flavor of the format used.

            > jupyter nbconvert --to html --template lab mynotebook.ipynb

            You can also pipe the output to stdout, rather than a file

            > jupyter nbconvert mynotebook.ipynb --stdout

            PDF is generated via latex

            > jupyter nbconvert mynotebook.ipynb --to pdf

            You can get (and serve) a Reveal.js-powered slideshow

            > jupyter nbconvert myslides.ipynb --to slides --post serve

            Multiple notebooks can be given at the command line in a couple of
            different ways:

            > jupyter nbconvert notebook*.ipynb
            > jupyter nbconvert notebook1.ipynb notebook2.ipynb

            or you can specify the notebooks list in a config file, containing::

                c.NbConvertApp.notebooks = ["my_notebook.ipynb"]

            > jupyter nbconvert --config mycfg.py

To see all available configurables, use `--help-all`.
